newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian actors attack PM on planned funding cuts.
newsitem.headline: Australian actors attack PM on planned funding cuts.

text.p: Australian Oscar winner Geoffrey Rush and other top Australian actors and producers such as Nicole Kidman and Scott Hicks joined forces on Friday to attack government plans to drastically cut film funding.

A letter to Prime Minister John Howard signed by actors, producers, directors and industry bodies said the proposed cuts, due out in the 1996/97 budget in May, would have a crippling effect on the industry and lead to a brain drain to Hollywood.

The government is expected to almost halve the annual A$140 million (US$109 million) funding to Australia's film and television industry, a spokeswoman for industry union the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance.

"In a year in which the Australia film industry has garnered huge international repect with the success of 'Shine'...and two Oscar winners in Geoffrey Rush and John Seale, it seems quite incomprehensible why treasury and finance are pushing for such draconian cuts," the film industry letter said.
Rush collected the best actor Oscar at the Academy Awards for his part in the Australian film "Shine" and Seale won the best cinematography award for his work on the "The English Patient".

"Inevitably, the cuts will lead to a rapid downturn in production and consequent unemployment, shake investor confidence in Australia's audiovisual industries and lead to a brain drain of talent to Hollywood," the letter said.

"The industry is fully aware that your government has a mandate for fiscal responsibility but the cuts suggested would have a crippling effect, both commercially and artistically, on the industry," it said.

The letter was signed by 19 of Australia's top actors and producers which included Rush and "Shine" director Hicks, Kidman, Judy Davis, Greta Scacchi, Sam Neill, "Babe" producer George Miller and "Babe" director Chris Noonan.

The proposed film funding cuts are totally counter to the year-old conservative government's arts policy titled "For Art's Sake", which promised to maintain existing levels of government funding to Australia's film and television industries.
The cuts also represent a rejection of a government commissioned review of the film industry released in February, which recommended that the current level of industry funding being maintained.
